title.narrative: Integrating VCT with Home Based Care

description.narrative:
St. Francis Community development Programme (FRACODEP) implements an HIV and AIDS home based care (HBC) project for people living with HIV and AIDS (PLWHA) in the three parishes; St. Paul, Rang’ala and Nyango’oma. This community based project is implemented in the 2 parishes of Rang’ala and Nyang’oma in the Archdiocese of Kisumu, which serve approximately 337,060 people. These parishes were selected due to their remote geographical locations and because the parishes comprise vast areas with very limited existing health care services. The project provides new Voluntary Counselling and Testing (VCT) services and promotes family and community involvement in home based care for people infected with and affected by HIV and AIDS. It offers people living with HIV and AIDS in the rural areas an opportunity to access quality care and support through a network of community volunteers recruited through existing and newly formed women’s groups. The project has 11 qualified staff who are supported by over 500 active volunteers, drawn mostly from women’s groups in the communities.
New infections and re-infection of HIV continue to occur despite various interventions. VCT has a crucial role to play as the entry point to HIV prevention and care. Availability and accessibility to VCTs has facilitated early diagnosis and timely treatment. Clients who have tested positive continue to receive care and support and live positively, while those who test negative are encouraged to maintain their positive status. The VCTs services have ensured effective uptake and follow up services including counselling, drug adherence and home based care; hence the delivery of a complete home based care package; and sustainability of the clients and the project. It is anticipated that HIV testing through VCTs will enhance people’s knowledge of their HIV status, behaviour change, improved physical status of clients, increased acceptance of HIV status, reduced stigma at individual, family and community level, disclosure, and positive living.
The project targeted to reach approximately 3,200 people through provision of VCT related services and has been successful ensuring mobile VCT service penetrates clients who did not have courage to test in public health institutions for fear of stigma. This has subsequently increased the uptake of VCT services. Post-test clubs and support group formation enhanced behaviour change among the community members as well as positive living among the PLHIV. Interaction between the positive and negative people in the groups has led to reduced stigma levels within the community.
During this period the project will continue to ensure provision of quality services to the community through trainings, counselling, testing, treatment, psychosocial support and networking with other stakeholders.
